title_en: The Rise of Organized Retail Crime at Big Box Stores
title_zh: 有组织零售犯罪的兴起：对话 Home Depot 资产保护副总裁 Scott Glenn
subtitle_zh: Home Depot 资产保护专家 Scott Glenn 拆解有组织零售犯罪、损耗统计与销赃链条。
summary_zh: 本期 Odd Lots 中，Tracy Alloway 与 Joe Weisenthal 对话 The Home Depot 负责资产保护（asset protection）的副总裁 Scott Glenn，拆解有组织零售犯罪（organized retail crime）。节目从货物盗窃讲起——窃贼伪造承运商身份提走整车库存，再到 Bloomberg 报道的现代火车大劫案与疫情后入店行窃（shoplifting）抬头、门店把商品锁进柜子的无奈。Glenn 解释损耗（shrink）的构成：Home Depot 约 30% 属运营性、行政性的自身损耗，其余多来自恶意行为；并勾勒出 booster（行窃者）把货交给 fence（销赃者）、再由后者清洗并转卖的完整链条，其中不少行窃者是受人指使、按清单跨店作案。他坦言给电钻等商品加装防盗模块（bricking）难以规模化，还谈到全渠道支付欺诈、礼品卡与退货欺诈、Meta 等平台上的销赃，以及 Flock 摄像头引发的公众反弹。Glenn 对立法与执法意愿转向乐观，主持人则反思犯罪像打地鼠（whack-a-mole）般不断向线上迁移，技术往往跑在制度前面。

turns.en: Hello, Odd Lodge listeners. I'm Joe Wiesenthal.
turns.zh: Hello，Odd Lots 的听众们，我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: We're the hosts of the Odd Lodge podcast, and we've got something exciting for you.
turns.zh: 我们是 Odd Lots 播客的主持人，今天有个令人兴奋的消息要告诉大家。

turns.en: That's right. So one of the best parts of hosting our podcast is we get to actually meet and interact with our listeners. And we know we have some listeners over in Los Angeles.
turns.zh: 没错。做这档播客主持人最棒的一点，就是我们能真正跟听众见面、互动。我们知道在 Los Angeles 那边也有一些听众。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: So if you're in L.A., we're going to be recording a live show, some live recordings at the Vermont Theater in Hollywood on September 17th.
turns.zh: 所以如果你在 L.A.，我们将在 9 月 17 日于 Hollywood 的 Vermont Theater 录制一场现场节目、做一些现场录制。

turns.en: We have some really exciting guests lined up, have some really great conversations planned. So go ahead and get your tickets. You can find those over at Bloomberg.com forward slash oddlots or click the link below in the show notes and come and say hi when you're there.
turns.zh: 我们邀请了几位非常令人期待的嘉宾，也策划了几场很棒的对话。所以赶紧去订票吧。你可以在 Bloomberg.com 斜杠 oddlots 上找到，或者点击节目备注下方的链接，到时候到现场来跟我们打个招呼。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios，播客、广播、新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Thoughts Podcast. I'm Traci Allaway.
turns.zh: Hello，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: Joe, we did an episode recently with Reid Lustelo, the chief marketing officer over at the Truck Parking Club.
turns.zh: Joe，我们最近做了一期节目，嘉宾是 Truck Parking Club 的首席营销官（chief marketing officer）Reid Lustelo。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And that was a great episode about the— Super fun. The rebound in trucking. But he mentioned one thing and he did it in a sort of offhand way. And it really piqued my interest. He basically said that cargo theft had become this huge deal. And it wasn't just, you know, some guys stealing boxes off the back of trucks, which is kind of what I have in my head.
turns.zh: 那是一期很棒的节目，讲的是——特别有意思——卡车运输业的复苏。但他提到一件事，而且是用一种很随口的方式说的，却真正勾起了我的兴趣。他基本上是说，货物盗窃（cargo theft）已经成了一件大事。而且它不只是，你知道，几个人从卡车后头偷箱子——那差不多是我脑子里原本的印象。

turns.en: Same.
turns.zh: 我也是。

turns.en: It was people spoofing actual carriers or pretending to be a carrier and then picking up entire cargo loads of inventory.
turns.zh: 而是有人伪造真实承运商的身份，或者假扮成承运商，然后把整整一车货物的库存提走。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And presumably reselling it.
turns.zh: 然后大概是拿去转卖。

turns.en: No, that totally blew my mind. I mean, it makes sense, right? Like, okay, if we're talking in the U.S., there's tens of thousands of trucking companies. And so the degree to which any shipper could really know any carrier is probably kind of loose, et cetera. It's like, yeah, why not just sort of like spring up one day and you know, get some shipments and then take them on your own way. It makes a lot of sense, but definitely not what I would have had in mind, as you said, about what a cargo theft meant up until that point.
turns.zh: 不，这完全颠覆了我的认知。我是说，这讲得通，对吧？比如，好，如果我们以美国来说，有数万家卡车运输公司。所以任何托运人能真正了解某个承运商的程度，大概都是相当松散的，等等。就好像，是啊，为什么不干脆某天突然冒出来，拿到一些货物，然后按自己的路子把它们带走。这非常讲得通，但绝对不是我原本——像你说的——在那之前对货物盗窃这个词的想象。

turns.en: Well, since then, I keep seeing these headlines popping up. There was a great Bloomberg story the other day actually called The Great Modern Train Robbery Thieves Steal $ 200 Million a Year Off of Railway Cars. And so you can see, like, This seems to be a big deal. We know, living in New York, that it feels like shoplifting has become a bigger deal in recent years after the pandemic. And we can debate whether or not the statistics bear that out. But certainly, if you walk down the street and you go into our local Duane Reade, everything's locked up, right?
turns.zh: 嗯，从那以后，我就不停看到这类标题冒出来。前几天其实有一篇很棒的 Bloomberg 报道，叫《伟大的现代火车大劫案：窃贼每年从铁路车厢上偷走 2 亿美元》（The Great Modern Train Robbery: Thieves Steal $200 Million a Year Off of Railway Cars）。所以你能看出来，这似乎是件大事。我们住在 New York，知道感觉上在疫情之后这几年，入店行窃（shoplifting）变成了一件更严重的事。我们可以争论统计数据是否支持这一点。但可以肯定的是，如果你走上街，走进我们本地的 Duane Reade，所有东西都锁起来了，对吧？

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: That's the sort of core thing. There's probably various ways to massage statistics and all kinds of stuff.
turns.zh: 这就是那个核心的东西。可能有各种办法去修饰统计数据之类的。

turns.en: But whatever.
turns.zh: 但不管怎样。

turns.en: It's not good. I see them locking this stuff up. They're locking it up. They must know that customers, by and large, hate it, right? They must know that it decreases labor productivity, having to have staffers in the store.
turns.zh: 这不好。我看到他们把这些东西锁起来。他们确实锁起来了。他们一定知道顾客大体上是讨厌这样的，对吧？他们一定知道这会降低劳动生产率，因为得让员工守在店里。

turns.en: You have to ring the bell and wait.
turns.zh: 你得按铃，然后等着。

turns.en: Yeah, get a deodorant. They can't think that that's a great operation. So if they're doing it. I presume there are some real issues there.
turns.zh: 对，就为了买一支除臭剂。他们不可能觉得这是什么好的运营方式。所以既然他们这么做了，我猜那里确实存在一些真问题。

turns.en: Well, we're going to get into all of it today. We'll do the sort of low level locking stuff up on shelves all the way to the high level pretending to be an entire trucking company and stealing someone's inventory that way. And I'm glad to say we have the perfect guest to try to understand all of this. We're going to be speaking with Scott Glenn. He is the vice president of asset protection over at The Home Depot and an organized retail crime expert. So truly the perfect person to speak to. Scott, thank you so much for coming on Odd Lots.
turns.zh: 嗯，今天我们要把这一切都聊个遍。从那种低端的、把货架上的东西锁起来，一直到高端的、假扮成一整家卡车运输公司、用这种方式偷走别人库存的做法。而且我很高兴地说，我们请到了理解这一切的完美嘉宾。我们要对话的是 Scott Glenn。他是 The Home Depot 负责资产保护（asset protection）的副总裁，也是有组织零售犯罪（organized retail crime）方面的专家。所以真的是最合适的对话人选。Scott，非常感谢你来上 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Yeah, thanks, guys.
turns.zh: 好，谢谢你们。

turns.en: Thanks for having me. I appreciate the expert designation. I'm not so sure I can live up to that, but I'll do my best.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请我。我很感激这个“专家”的称号。我不太确定自己能不能担得起，但我会尽力。

turns.en: I love that you're wearing the Home Depot apron as well.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你今天还穿着 Home Depot 的围裙。

turns.en: Yeah, look, it's part of our culture. It's part of what we are.
turns.zh: 是啊，你看，这是我们文化的一部分，是我们身份的一部分。

turns.en: You can see our values over our heart is an intentional thing. Today's earnings day for Home Depot, and so we're all supporting the cause.
turns.zh: 你能看到我们把这些价值观印在心口的位置，这是有意为之的。今天是 Home Depot 的财报日，所以我们都在为这件事加油。

turns.en: All right, first question, and then we can get into maybe more serious topics. But what's the most stolen item from Home Depot?
turns.zh: 好，先来第一个问题，然后我们再聊一些也许更严肃的话题。Home Depot 被偷得最多的商品是什么？

turns.en: Volume or dollars?
turns.zh: 按数量还是按金额？

turns.en: Well, let's do both.
turns.zh: 嗯，两个都说吧。

turns.en: Let's do both.
turns.zh: 两个都说吧。

turns.en: So I would say volume, it's typically something like a power drill.
turns.zh: 那么按数量的话，通常是像电钻（power drill）这类东西。

turns.en: You see a lot of that.
turns.zh: 你会看到很多这种情况。

turns.en: And then when you start to get into dollars, believe it or not, copper and wire have a lot of the commodity.
turns.zh: 而当你开始按金额算的话，信不信由你，铜和电线这类商品占了很大一部分……

turns.en: Value out there.
turns.zh: ……的价值。

turns.en: And so we see people come in, they'll take a lot of that stuff out of the building and try to resell it or use it on jobs, things like that. But yeah, so certainly those are certainly two of the bigger ones.
turns.zh: 所以我们会看到有人进来，把大量这类东西搬出店外，试图转卖，或者拿去工地上用，等等。但是的，所以这两样肯定是占比较大的。

turns.en: Joe, someone broke into... There's a museum close to where I am in Connecticut called the Nathan Hale Museum, an old colonial homestead. Someone broke into it recently and stole a bunch of copper pipes.
turns.zh: Joe，有人闯进了……我住的 Connecticut 附近有一座博物馆，叫 Nathan Hale Museum，是一处古老的殖民地时期宅邸。最近有人闯进去，偷走了一堆铜管。

turns.en: Are you serious? Like old pipes that were.
turns.zh: 你认真的吗？就是那种老管子？

turns.en: Apparently it was in the house next to it, but... It was still pretty upsetting for everyone, you know, a historic home getting.
turns.zh: 据说其实是旁边那栋房子，但……对大家来说还是挺难受的，你知道，一栋历史建筑被……

turns.en: Hit for copper.
turns.zh: 为了铜被下手。

turns.en: It happens everywhere. When I joined Home Depot eight years ago and I moved into.
turns.zh: 这种事到处都有。八年前我加入 Home Depot，搬进……

turns.en: My house, between the time I closed on my house and the time that I moved into the house, they took all the copper out of the HVAC units and all the pieces of it. So it is definitely a commodity that fluctuates in price. And when the price goes up, it becomes really valuable to the bad guys.
turns.zh: 我的房子，就在我完成过户和真正搬进去之间那段时间，他们把暖通空调（HVAC）机组里所有的铜以及各个部件都拆走了。所以它确实是一种价格会波动的商品。当价格上涨时，它对那些坏人就变得非常值钱。

turns.en: Well, that's actually a great thing. So you mentioned you've been at the Home Depot for eight years. But why don't you give us a quick like sort of overview of your career, what your role is, why we're talking to you, like what's been the main thing that have landed you in this chair?
turns.zh: 嗯，这其实是个很好的引子。你提到你在 Home Depot 待了八年。不如快速给我们讲讲你的职业生涯概况，你的角色是什么，我们为什么要跟你聊，是什么主要的经历让你坐到了今天这个位置？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: So I would tell you, surprised that I'm in this chair. I went to school to be an architect when I was going into college and realized that I wasn't very good at math. So I decided to maybe go work for the FBI. And I got into the criminal justice side of the business. I was always fascinated by the law. I ended up going to law school after college and did that route. But I started working with the Treasury Department right out of law school and worked for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. realized that I did not like government service.
turns.zh: 我会说，我自己都惊讶能坐在这个位置上。上大学时我本想学建筑，结果发现自己数学不太好。所以我想，那不如去 FBI 工作吧。于是我进入了刑事司法（criminal justice）这一行。我一直对法律很着迷。大学毕业后我最终上了法学院，走了那条路。但一出法学院我就进了财政部（Treasury Department），在烟酒枪炮管理局（Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms）工作。然后我意识到自己并不喜欢政府工作。

turns.en: It just wasn't my gig.
turns.zh: 那压根不是我的菜。

turns.en: It wasn't what I wanted to do forever. And so I had during summers, during school, I had worked at Target and caught shoplifters. So just kind of a side, you know, make some money gig. And luckily, I was able to get back my foot in the door with Target after I left the government and worked for them and just worked my way up through the ranks. So Been here, been at Kohl's department stores for 10 years. I was at Sears for 10 years as a CSO. And then I came back here to Home Depot eight years ago.
turns.zh: 那不是我想要做一辈子的事。上学时我在暑假打过工，在 Target 抓过入店行窃者，就是一份兼职、赚点外快的活儿。幸运的是，我离开政府后又能重新在 Target 站住脚，为他们工作，一路晋升上来。所以我在这一行待过，在 Kohl's 百货干了 10 年，在 Sears 干了 10 年、担任首席安全官（CSO）。然后八年前我又回到了 Home Depot。

turns.en: So before we go any further, why don't we define our terms? When we talk about retail theft, I imagine this covers a range of activities from, you know, someone innocently perhaps forgetting to scan their deodorant at self-checkout to really organized, seemingly very ambitious heist. What are we talking about exactly here? How do you kind of categorize retail theft in your head?
turns.zh: 那在我们继续之前，不如先把概念定义清楚？当我们谈零售盗窃（retail theft）时，我想它涵盖了一系列行为，从有人也许无辜地在自助结账时忘了扫他的除臭剂，到真正有组织、看起来野心很大的劫案。我们这里到底在说什么？你脑子里是怎么给零售盗窃分类的？

turns.en: Yeah, it's a spectrum to your point. There's definitely low level opportunistic, I'll even call it the need shoplifters that are out there. They just can't afford things.
turns.zh: 对，就像你说的，这是一个谱系。确实存在低端的、机会主义的，我甚至称之为“需求型”行窃者，他们就在那儿。他们只是买不起这些东西。

turns.en: And we know that happens.
turns.zh: 我们知道这种情况会发生。

turns.en: And that's not what I would say acceptable to us, but it's also not our focus. It's not the place where we spend a lot of our energy and our tactics up to the most sophisticated criminal organizations that are out there. And I mean, sophisticated, cartel-related, transnational gang-related international organizations whose sole existence is to monetize theft to do other bad things, whether that's money laundering, drug trafficking, human trafficking. And these are absolutely known things that are happening out there. So there's a lot of space in between that, and it runs the gamut. But we tend to focus our time and our energy and our resources on the higher end.
turns.zh: 这并不是说这对我们而言可以接受，但它也不是我们的重点。它不是我们投入大量精力和手段去对付的地方，一直往上到那些最老练的犯罪组织。我说的老练，是指与贩毒集团（cartel）相关、跨国的、与帮派相关的国际组织，它们存在的唯一目的就是把盗窃变现，去做其他坏事，无论是洗钱（money laundering）、贩毒（drug trafficking）还是人口贩卖（human trafficking）。这些都是确凿发生在外面、已知的事情。所以这中间有很大一片空间，涵盖了各种情形。但我们往往把时间、精力和资源集中在更高端的那一头。

turns.en: While we're in the business of defining terms here, I think this is helpful. A word like shrinkage is one that comes up. Would shrinkage only apply to, okay, the person who walks into a store and manages to walk out with a power drill or something like that? Or is it counted in shrinkage statistics if it's like a very– complex heist of an entire truck that never makes it to the destination.
turns.zh: 既然我们在做定义术语这件事，我觉得这很有帮助。像损耗（shrinkage）这样的词会被提到。损耗是否只适用于那种走进店里、想办法带着一把电钻之类的东西走出来的人？还是说，如果是一整车货物极其复杂的劫案、货车根本没到目的地，这也会被计入损耗统计？

turns.en: When we talk about shrink in retail, we're talking about at the end of the day, I have inventory on my books. And when I physically go to count that inventory, it's not there. There's a lot of different ways that could happen. That is not just the bad guys coming in and stealing stuff. So when we talk about things within our world here, when I talk with our leadership and I talk to our board, We break it out into what we call operational or controllable administrative types of strength, and then what we call the malicious. And another way to look at that is might be like things we do to ourself versus things people do to us. And that's the way we tend to categorize that ratio.
turns.zh: 当我们谈零售业里的损耗（shrink）时，我们说的是，归根结底，我账面上有库存，而当我实际去盘点这些库存时，它不在了。这有很多种不同的发生方式，不只是坏人进来偷东西。所以在我们的世界里谈这些事时，当我和我们的领导层、和我们的董事会谈时，我们把它拆分成我们所说的运营性或可控的、行政类的损耗（operational/administrative shrink），以及我们所说的恶意损耗（malicious）。另一种看法就像是“我们自己造成的”对“别人对我们造成的”。这就是我们通常给这个比例分类的方式。

turns.en: And for us.
turns.zh: 而对我们来说。

turns.en: I'm not going to say this is for everybody at retail, but for us, we're pretty good at controlling the operational side of the business. So about 30 percent of our shrink is falls into that operational administrative things we do to ourself type of category. And then the balance of it falls into more of the malicious side or things that people do to us.
turns.zh: 我不会说这对所有零售商都适用，但对我们来说，我们在控制业务的运营这一侧做得相当好。所以我们大约 30% 的损耗属于那种运营性、行政性的、我们自己造成的类别。剩下的则更多属于恶意的一侧，也就是别人对我们造成的。

turns.en: That's very helpful. And then one more question on this in the broader category of retail theft. Do you have a split on how much happens in store versus somewhere else, whether it's one of the distribution center, warehouse, et cetera, versus somewhere else on the supply chain?
turns.zh: 这非常有帮助。那么在这个更大的零售盗窃范畴里再问一个问题。对于多少发生在店内、多少发生在别处——无论是配送中心、仓库等等，还是供应链上的其他地方——你有没有一个划分的比例？

turns.en: Yeah, so we actually break out our shrink in the supply chain separately. Then we break out our shrink in the retail environments versus the way we break out our shrink in our online environment. So we actually have three different buckets of where the shrink can happen that roll up to our larger. Now, in the supply chain, you can have operational, financial, and malicious shrink. In the stores, you can have operational, financial, and malicious shrink. And online, you can have operational, financial.
turns.zh: 对，所以我们其实是把供应链里的损耗单独拆出来。然后我们把零售环境里的损耗，跟线上环境里损耗的拆分方式分开来看。所以我们实际上有三个不同的桶，损耗可能发生在这些地方，再汇总到我们更大的总数里。在供应链里，你可能有运营性、财务性和恶意的损耗。在门店里，你可能有运营性、财务性和恶意的损耗。在线上，你可能有运营性、财务性……

turns.en: And malicious shrink.
turns.zh: 以及恶意的损耗。

turns.en: So that all rolls up to the big number. But the biggest chunk of it, to your point, does exist in the 2,400 stores, retail stores that we have out there.
turns.zh: 所以这些全都汇总成那个大数字。但就像你说的，其中最大的一块确实存在于我们外面那 2,400 家零售门店里。

turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.en: So give us a sense of the overall shrink problem versus how much of it is malicious, how much of it is operational across the industry. And is it true that that retail theft has become more of an issue. Because again, you see these statistics, you see the headlines target closing two stores because of rising crime, or you see a company come out and say, oh, our shrink has gone up this year. But to your point, it could be because maybe they're just worse at keeping track of their inventory than they were the year before. So give us some context around how big a problem this is and whether or not it's been getting worse.
turns.zh: 那么给我们讲讲，相对于整个行业里有多少是恶意的、有多少是运营性的，整体损耗问题有多大。零售盗窃是不是真的变成了一个更严重的问题？因为话说回来，你会看到这些统计数据、这些标题，比如 Target 因为犯罪上升而关闭两家门店，或者你看到某家公司出来说“哦，我们今年的损耗上升了”。但就像你说的，这可能是因为他们只是比上一年更不擅长追踪自己的库存了。所以给我们一些背景，这个问题到底有多大，它是不是一直在恶化。

turns.en: You're getting to probably the most debated question in retail asset protection, loss prevention, which is... And I wish I could give you a clean answer on that.
turns.zh: 你问到的可能是零售资产保护（asset protection）、防损（loss prevention）领域里最有争议的问题，那就是……我真希望能给你一个干净利落的答案。

turns.en: I can't. I can tell you... Maybe I'll start at the top and say... How big is it? It's in the billions.
turns.zh: 我不能。我可以告诉你……也许我先从最上面说起……它有多大？以十亿计。

turns.en: It's in the tens of billions. The shrink problem. There's a lot of different estimates out there. Our cohorts, my peers, my friends and peer retailers, we all talk about this.
turns.zh: 是几百亿美元。这个损耗问题。外面有很多不同的估计。我们的同行、我的同业、我的朋友和其他零售商，我们都在谈论这个。

turns.en: We work with Rilo. We work with NRF.
turns.zh: 我们与 Rilo 合作。我们也与 NRF（美国零售联合会，National Retail Federation）合作。

turns.en: We work with all to try to get the best estimates on what this number is, but how people categorize shrink. What somebody calls operational shrink versus administrative versus malicious can vary by retailers. And so you've got the retail component of... We are a retail accounting operation. There are companies that are on cost accounting. And so making that transition between the dollars and how do you include markup and to get to a number, very, very complicated number.
turns.zh: 我们与所有这些机构合作，试图对这个数字得出最好的估计，但人们如何归类损耗——有人称之为运营性损耗、行政性损耗还是恶意损耗——因零售商而异。所以你有零售这一块……我们采用的是零售会计（retail accounting）的方式。有些公司用的是成本会计（cost accounting）。所以在金额之间做转换、如何把加价（markup）算进去、最终得出一个数字，是非常非常复杂的一个数字。

turns.en: What I can tell you is that.
turns.zh: 我能告诉你的是。

turns.en: There's these numbers that have been around as long as I've been doing this in retail, which is like 40% of shrink on the malicious side is done by associates working for the company.
turns.zh: 有些数字，自从我在零售业干这行以来就一直存在，比如恶意损耗那一侧有 40% 是公司自己的员工（associates）干的。

turns.en: They cause 40% of your loss.
turns.zh: 他们造成了你 40% 的损失。

turns.en: 35% are people walking into your store and causing it. And 20, 25, whatever the balance is, is that self-inflicted operational administrative types of shrink. And so Those numbers add flow. They go every year. There's surveys that are done. They might go up a couple of percentage. They might go down a couple of percentages. What I can speak to is when I got here at Home Depot in 2018, I wasn't even really a big believer in what you would call the organized retail crime problem. Also pre-COVID, also before Omni really took off and has blown up to what it is here. Places where you can resell very impersonally.
turns.zh: 35% 是走进你店里造成损耗的人。而 20、25，不管剩下多少，是那种自己造成的运营性、行政性损耗。所以这些数字会流动，每年都会变。有做过一些调查。它们可能上升几个百分点，也可能下降几个百分点。我能讲的是，2018 年我刚到 Home Depot 时，我甚至并不太相信你们所说的那个有组织零售犯罪（organized retail crime）问题。那也是在新冠之前，也是在全渠道（omni）真正起飞、爆发成今天这个样子之前。那些你可以非常非人格化地转卖商品的地方。

turns.en: Wait, what's Omni?
turns.zh: 等等，什么是 Omni？

turns.en: Online.
turns.zh: 线上。

turns.en: Online sales.
turns.zh: 线上销售。

turns.en: Sorry.
turns.zh: 抱歉。

turns.en: Omni Channel. Sorry.
turns.zh: 全渠道（omni channel）。抱歉。

turns.en: But when you think about the kinetics of all that and how that's changed over time, and I would tell you that I have become a believer in one, organized retail crime exists.
turns.zh: 但当你想到这一切的动态、以及它随时间发生的变化，我会告诉你，我已经变成一个相信者：第一，有组织零售犯罪确实存在。

turns.en: It's become more lucrative. It's become more pervasive. And it's become more dangerous.
turns.zh: 它变得更赚钱，更普遍，也更危险。

turns.en: When it comes to how it impacts the customers and the associates in the stores. So while those numbers have generally estimated stayed in the kind of same buckets, I believe they're starting to drift up. And I also believe since COVID, they've been underreported. And so I think that there's a big piece of that, that it's just not necessarily reflecting in all the numbers that you see showing up in police reporting, FBI uniform crime reports, things of that nature.
turns.zh: 就它如何影响店里的顾客和员工而言。所以，尽管那些数字大体上估计还停留在差不多相同的桶里，我相信它们开始往上漂移。而且我也相信，自新冠以来，它们被低报了。所以我认为其中有一大块，并不一定反映在你看到的所有数字里，比如警方报案、FBI 统一犯罪报告（FBI uniform crime reports）之类。

turns.en: So maybe this is a good opportunity to sort of dive into some details. But you said earlier in the episode that you're more interested in the sort of more sophisticated, organized drivers of shrink than perhaps a random person who maybe they can't afford an item, etc. Can you talk to us about in a given theft, etc., someone goes into a store and they walk out or they take something that they didn't pay for. What are the fingerprints that look like, okay, this we have reason to believe was part of something sophisticated and organized versus this is like, yeah, we don't support that, but it's one random person and it's not going to be the main thing we prioritize.
turns.zh: 那也许这是深入一些细节的好机会。你前面在节目里说，相比于某个可能买不起某件商品的随机个人，你对那些更老练、更有组织的损耗驱动因素更感兴趣。你能跟我们谈谈吗，在某一起盗窃中，有人走进店里然后走出来、或者拿走没付钱的东西。那些“指纹”是什么样的——就是“好，我们有理由相信这是某个老练、有组织行动的一部分”，对立于“是啊，我们不认可这种行为，但这只是一个随机的个人，不会是我们要优先处理的主要目标”。

turns.en: Yeah, you guys asked some great questions to get right into the details of how some of this becomes difficult.
turns.zh: 是啊，你们问的问题很棒，直接切入了这一切为什么在细节上会变得困难。

turns.en: So in an individual instance, it's almost impossible.
turns.zh: 所以在单个案例里，这几乎是不可能的。

turns.en: If you talk to somebody, if we have people in our stores, their whole job is to stop theft. That's what they do, that they detain people, they prosecute, they work with the law enforcement, and they deal with that. And then we have groups of people here in Atlanta whose job is to handle the more sophisticated components of this.
turns.zh: 如果你跟某个人谈，如果我们店里有人，他们的整个工作就是阻止盗窃。这就是他们做的事：他们拘留人、提起诉讼、与执法部门合作、处理这些。然后我们在 Atlanta 这里有一批人，他们的工作是处理这件事里更老练的那部分。

turns.en: Piece of it.
turns.zh: 部分。

turns.en: But it all starts locally. It all starts in the stores. And so some of that is, hey, I see somebody steal that drill. And you sit down and have a conversation with that person before they end up going to jail. And they were really using it to work on a project on their deck on their house.
turns.zh: 但一切都始于本地，始于门店。所以有些情况是，嘿，我看到有人偷了那把电钻。然后在这个人最终进监狱之前，你坐下来跟他谈一谈。而他真的是想拿它去修缮自家房子上的露台。

turns.en: Whereas you might have.
turns.zh: 而另一些情况你可能会有。

turns.en: That conversation with them and say, yeah, I was asked to come in and steal this and I was going to go take it to another place. And I was going to get money for that or I was going to get drugs for that or I was going to get something and I was going to get given a list to go to another store and go get something else. And so we cultivate that intelligence. We cultivate those resources and report that back to our folks here. who are organized retail crime experts and do this for a living, most of whom are former federal law enforcement agents or law enforcement agents at state and local agencies. And their job is to figure out which is the wheat and which is the chaff and what are the things that are the most important thing for us to go. So we have video analytics, we have other technologies that we work on to kind of say, okay, Now, I know this person.
turns.zh: 跟他谈的时候，他会说，是啊，我是被人叫进来偷这个的，我本来要把它带到另一个地方去。我会因此拿到钱，或者拿到毒品，或者拿到别的东西，而且他们会给我一份清单，让我去另一家店拿别的东西。所以我们会培养这类情报，积累这些资源，并把它汇报给我们这边的人——他们是有组织零售犯罪方面的专家，以此为业，其中大多数是前联邦执法人员，或者州和地方机构的执法人员。他们的工作就是分辨哪些是麦、哪些是糠，弄清楚对我们来说最重要的是去追查什么。所以我们有视频分析（video analytics），还有其他我们研发的技术，用来判断，好，现在我认识这个人了。

turns.en: I know this car. I know this vehicle.
turns.zh: 我认识这辆车。我认识这台车。

turns.en: I've seen them in store A. Now, I've seen them in store B. We've got a report from that building that says Johnny with driver's license 123456 has been in now four stores apprehended for theft because... they're going to get apprehended. They might be put in jail and they'll be out the next day. You know, they're going to make bail or there's going to be no cash bail or whatever the case may be. And they're just going to go back to doing what they're doing. And so that's how we try to like stitch these cases together and understand which ones are the ones that are more valuable to pull on versus the ones that are like, this is really a one-time occurrence and this is not something that we need to spend a lot of resources on.
turns.zh: 我在 A 店见过他们，现在我在 B 店也见过他们。我们拿到一份来自那栋楼的报告，说驾照号 123456 的 Johnny 现在已经进了四家店、因盗窃被抓，因为……他们就是会被抓。他们可能被关进监狱，第二天就出来了。你知道，他们会保释出来，或者根本没有现金保释，或者不管是什么情况。然后他们就会回去继续干他们干的事。所以这就是我们试图把这些案子串起来、弄清楚哪些案子更值得深挖的方式，对立于那些“这真的只是一次性事件、我们不需要投入大量资源”的案子。

turns.en: To what degree do you actually work with the police? Because when you talk about, well, we observe these people going to different stores and we try to see if we can identify patterns and stitch the sort of ring together. That sounds like something the police should be doing.
turns.zh: 你们实际上在多大程度上与警方合作？因为当你说，嗯，我们观察到这些人跑去不同的门店，我们试着看能不能识别出模式、把这个团伙串起来。这听起来像是警察应该做的事。

turns.en: Sometimes it's hard enough to get the police to show up. And I'm not blaming in this case. I mean, we know that police departments are under-resourced, stretched very thin. When you talk about retail theft versus robbery versus carjacking versus murder and the escalation hierarchy, where are they going to spend their time right so they're they're not going to always be able to have the capability to come to our store and deal with this so i would tell you our i'll call it our internal behind the scenes as we our job is to do the work for them our job is to hand them a case file that is 80 complete that says i've given you everything that i can possibly do for you to then walk into a judge get a search warrant get an arrest warrant do everything that i can't do and i they're going to respect that. They're going to say, if I don't have to do all the hard work, I don't have to do all the behind-the-scenes labor, and all I've got to do is walk in front of a judge and say, this is a great case, and we believe everything that's here, and put their hand up and swear on the Bible, then they're going to take those cases much more regularly than somebody that's kind of saying, hey, you just go figure it out for me.
turns.zh: 有时候连让警察出到场都够难的。这一点我不是在责怪谁。我是说，我们知道警察部门资源不足、被拉得非常薄。当你把零售盗窃跟抢劫、跟劫车、跟谋杀放在一起，还有那个升级等级，他们会把时间花在哪里，对吧？所以他们并不总是有能力到我们店里来处理这件事。所以我会告诉你，我称之为我们内部幕后的做法是：我们的工作是替他们把活干了，我们的工作是交给他们一份已经完成 80% 的案卷，上面写着“我已经把我能做的一切都给你了，接下来你去见法官、拿搜查令、拿逮捕令，做那些我做不了的事”。他们会尊重这一点。他们会说，如果我不用做所有苦活、不用做所有幕后的工作，我要做的只是走到法官面前说“这是个很棒的案子，这里的一切我们都相信”，然后举手按着《圣经》宣誓，那么他们接手这类案子的频率，会比面对那种只会说“嘿，你自己去查清楚”的人高得多。

turns.en: Just one more question on this. Is it true that some retailers... will not stop shoplifting until they observe the shoplifter getting to a certain threshold of goods stolen, because then they can go for like an actual meaningful charge.
turns.zh: 就这个再问一个问题。是不是真的有些零售商……在观察到行窃者偷到某个门槛的商品数量之前不会出手制止，因为那样他们才能提出一个真正有意义的指控？

turns.en: You know, I would be hard pressed to speak to that for what the policies of some of my compatriots are there. But what I would say is, is we don't do that. When people say that, I feel like they're kind of looking at things in a very narrow scope. And going back to our point earlier, this may be something where we're already working on this person. We know they've been in 50 stores over the last 30 days stealing from us. And if they walk out the door, it may be because we're going to go watch them go to where the fence is or where they're going to resell the product or where they're storing the product. That might be part of an operation versus a, hey, we're letting you go get to a threshold. And that's really what, you know, at least from our end, we're not trying to like build up big charges on people. We're trying to say, I want to get the complete picture of what's happening, because when I wrap this up, I want it to be completely wrapped up.
turns.zh: 你知道，要我去评论我一些同行的政策，我会很难开口。但我要说的是，我们不这么做。当人们那么说时，我觉得他们是在一个非常狭隘的范围内看问题。回到我们前面说的那点，这可能是我们已经在盯这个人的情况。我们知道他在过去 30 天里进了 50 家店偷我们的东西。而如果他走出门，可能是因为我们打算跟踪他，看他去销赃者（fence）那里、去转卖商品的地方，或者去存放商品的地方。那可能是某个行动的一部分，而不是“嘿，我们放你走、好让你达到某个门槛”。至少从我们这边来说，我们并不是想给人们堆砌重罪指控。我们想说的是，我要把正在发生的事的完整图景搞清楚，因为当我收网时，我要把它彻底了结。

turns.en: Intuitively, it seems like it would probably be pretty hard to prevent someone from like stealing a... a washer, like the little disc or something like that, you know, like put it in your jeans pockets or whatever. It seems like technology should make it very hard intuitively to steal a power drill because I imagine you could put tags on it that would set off alarms, that you could have video surveillance that could simply set off something if a person was in one aisle, trigger. I have to imagine it's not that hard to train a model to identify someone, take it off the shelf, and then that person makes a route out the store without ever having gone to the register. This seems solvable by technology alone. Why isn't it? What is it makes such that, A, it must still happen all the time, or B, It only gets stopped if a person at the end happens to notice it.
turns.zh: 凭直觉，要阻止某人偷一个……一个垫圈，就是那种小圆片之类的，你懂的，塞进牛仔裤口袋什么的，似乎会相当难。但凭直觉，技术应该会让偷一把电钻变得非常难，因为我想你可以在上面装标签，触发警报；你可以有视频监控，只要有人在某条过道里做了某个动作就能触发点什么。我不得不想，训练一个模型去识别某人把东西从货架上拿下来、然后那个人规划一条不出示收银台的路线走出店门，这应该不难。这看起来单靠技术就能解决。为什么没解决？是什么导致了，A，这种事仍然一直在发生，或者 B，只有当末端恰好有个人注意到时才会被制止？

turns.en: I love your thought process. That is a really expensive thought process.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你的思路。但那是一个非常烧钱的思路。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: And you think about a Home Depot store, 140,000 square feet of a working warehouse. to put the cameras that I would need to do that. And by the way, there are places where we do that. There are places, you know, in some aisles we're able to do that, but we have a lot of valuable stuff in our stores, in different parts of the store. At the front end, we have AI, you know, base cameras and We have a lot of different, I would say, video analytics that are continuing to evolve and we're really leaning into. But it is expensive and it's a lot of processing power. It's a lot of hardware that you have to put into your stores. We have some advantages with our scale and our size to be able to do some of that. Not everybody does, and certainly not everybody has. Sometimes it's a little bit of a tradeoff, like how much are you willing to take and shrink versus how much you would have to invest in hardware, capital expense, operating expenses to be able to put it to zero. I mean, the number we aspire to is zero. The number we'll get to is somewhere north of that.
turns.zh: 你想想一家 Home Depot 门店，14 万平方英尺的一个运转中的仓库。要装上我需要的那些摄像头才能做到那件事。而且顺便说一句，有些地方我们确实这么做了。有些地方，你知道，在某些过道里我们能做到，但我们店里有很多值钱的东西，分布在店里的不同区域。在前端，我们有基于 AI 的摄像头，还有很多不同的、我会说是视频分析的技术在持续演进，我们正在大力投入。但它很贵，需要大量算力，需要往店里投入大量硬件。凭我们的规模和体量，我们在做其中一些事情上有优势。不是每家都有，当然也不是每家都具备。有时候这有点像一个权衡：你愿意承受多少损耗，对立于你要投入多少硬件、资本支出（capital expense）、运营支出（operating expenses），才能把它降到零。我是说，我们追求的数字是零，而我们实际能达到的数字会在那个之上某处。

turns.en: But just like, what about tags and stuff that are, I mean, there are clothing items in many stores that have tags that will set off an alarm. Why at a level of a power drill, is that an insufficient technology to get the number to zero?
turns.zh: 但是，那标签之类的东西呢？我是说，很多店里的服装商品都有会触发警报的标签。为什么在电钻这个层面上，那种技术不足以把数字降到零？

turns.en: It's not insufficient. We've played around in the bricking of product space. When you think about the margins in some of these places, does it make sense to do it, to go have to redefine your entire production line for a Milwaukee drill in order to insert a technology, a Bluetooth chip of some sort?
turns.zh: 它并非不足。我们在给产品加装防盗模块（bricking）这个领域做过尝试。当你想到这些地方的一些利润率时，这么做是否划算——为了植入某种技术、某种蓝牙芯片，而不得不重新定义你一整条 Milwaukee 电钻的生产线？

turns.en: We've tried that. It's very, very hard to scale up.
turns.zh: 我们试过。这非常非常难以规模化。

turns.en: And again, you still have to put hardware in your stores to be able to detect those tags. that that's the piece that typically is very expensive. Again, none of this is impossible. It's just like there's always trade-offs and you're working towards that.
turns.zh: 而且话说回来，你仍然得在店里装硬件才能检测到那些标签。那一部分通常是非常昂贵的。再说一次，这些都不是不可能。只是永远存在权衡，你在朝那个方向努力。

turns.en: It's going to take some time.
turns.zh: 这需要一些时间。

turns.en: I mean, to be honest with you, RFID has a lot of promise in terms of tracking, not just the theft side of product, but like, Where is this product in the store?
turns.zh: 我是说，说实话，射频识别（RFID）在追踪方面很有前景，不只是商品的防盗这一侧，还比如，这件商品在店里的什么位置？

turns.en: Has it been sold?
turns.zh: 它卖出去了吗？

turns.en: What's the replenishment look like? How do you get your on-hands corrected? There's a ton of business opportunities on those pieces, but I think that RFID hardware costs have always been so expensive, it's almost impossible to put it in a Home Depot store where we have eight separate entrances.
turns.zh: 补货情况怎么样？你怎么修正你的在手库存（on-hands）？在这些方面存在大量商业机会，但我认为 RFID 的硬件成本一直太贵了，几乎不可能把它装进一家 Home Depot 门店——我们有八个独立的出入口。

turns.en: In and out of our building.
turns.zh: 进出我们的楼宇。

turns.en: How much of this is a liability issue in the sense that, okay, I can tag an item and I can hear an alarm ring if someone is going out with it without paying, but... There's still an issue over whether or not you want your employees, even your security guards, going after people who might actually fight back and be dangerous. And I'm sure we've all seen, you especially, Scott. the videos of some guy who just fills a massive shopping cart and walks out of the store with the security staff looking on.
turns.zh: 这其中有多少是一个责任（liability）问题，就是说，好，我可以给一件商品装标签，如果有人没付钱就带着它出去，我能听到警报响，但……仍然存在一个问题：你是否愿意让你的员工、甚至你的保安去追那些可能真的会反抗、可能有危险的人。我相信我们都见过——尤其是你，Scott——那种视频，某个人把一辆巨大的购物车装满，然后就这么走出店门，保安在一旁看着。

turns.en: It's the bigger issue than the financial, right? Like at the end of the day, there's a certain level of, we understand there's going to be some shrink in our stores. There's a certain cost of doing business. When you open up to the public, you're going to have some of this, this type of pieces of it. But this is the problem specifically with the organized retail crime folks, the professional criminals who, A lot of times they're using homeless folks, addicted folks, people that are maybe on the down and down low, and they are monetizing them to go in and do this. And their only thought process is, I'm leaving with this product because I need to get my money. I need to get my whatever. And they will do violent things. And they have done violent things. And not only has it happened in retail, it's happened specifically to us. And we've actually had people injured. We've had people killed in our stores in these types of incidents where that is just– we're not going to allow that. So our security folks, our asset protection people in stores– They're trained. They're trained not only on how to do what they do, but also how to de-escalate, how to observe and pull away from those situations when they start there. But we also have 400,000 store associates who are very passionate. They don't like to see stuff stolen. And we train them very clearly on like, you don't get involved with these things. You back away and we do give them the same, you know, a slightly different, but still de-escalation type training. Because that's the problem. I'll trade the shrink for the safety of the people every day of the week. And my leadership team and our board would back us on those decisions all day long. We're never, ever going to put people in jeopardy. Our associates and our customers are the number one priority.
turns.zh: 这是比财务更大的问题，对吧？归根结底，在某个层面上，我们明白店里会有一些损耗。这是做生意的一种成本。当你向公众敞开大门，你就会有一些这类东西。但这正是有组织零售犯罪那帮人、那些职业罪犯特有的问题：很多时候他们在利用无家可归的人、上瘾的人、也许处境非常低谷的人，把他们变现，让他们进去干这个。而他们脑子里唯一的想法就是，我要带着这件商品离开，因为我需要拿到我的钱、拿到我的什么。他们会做出暴力行为，而且他们已经做过暴力行为。这不仅发生在零售业，还专门发生在我们身上。我们真的有人受伤，甚至有人在我们的店里在这类事件中丧生，那是我们绝不允许的。所以我们的保安、我们店里的资产保护人员，他们是受过训练的。他们不仅受训如何做好本职工作，还受训如何缓和局势（de-escalate）、如何观察并在情况开始失控时抽身。但我们还有 40 万名门店员工，他们非常有激情，不喜欢看到东西被偷。我们非常明确地训练他们：你不介入这些事，你要退开。我们也给他们同样、你知道、略有不同、但仍然是缓和局势类型的培训。因为这就是问题所在。我每天都愿意用损耗去换人的安全。我的领导团队和我们的董事会会一直支持我们做这样的决定。我们绝不会、绝不会把人置于危险之中。我们的员工和顾客永远是第一位的。

turns.en: I've been hearing, we've been hearing about RFID tags. For 25 years now, I would have assumed that the price of this hardware would have come down dramatically such that you slap a little tag on and it's not very easy to remove. And then by the time you go through some gate or entrance, it sets off an alarm. Can you talk about why in 2026 that technology is still actually expensive and hard to scale?
turns.zh: 我一直听到、我们一直听到 RFID 标签的说法，到现在已经 25 年了。我本以为这种硬件的价格会大幅下降，以至于你贴上一个不易移除的小标签，然后当你经过某个闸口或入口时，它就触发警报。你能谈谈为什么到了 2026 年，这种技术实际上仍然昂贵、难以规模化吗？

turns.en: No, I can't.
turns.zh: 不，我谈不了。

turns.en: I don't understand it. It's your lips to God's ears, right? Like it's one of those things where I'm with you. And I will say a Home Depot environment, a little different. We are a hardware store with basically a Faraday cage of steel throughout our stores. We do a passive RFID does not work in our stores. You have to go to an active store. pinging RFID technology. We've tested it. We know it can work. Again, it's all about typically those.
turns.zh: 我也不理解。这是“你说出口、上帝听得见”的事，对吧？就像那种事情，我跟你站在一边。我会说 Home Depot 的环境有点不一样。我们是一家五金店，店里基本上到处是钢铁构成的法拉第笼（Faraday cage）。我们做过——被动式 RFID 在我们店里不管用。你必须用主动式、会主动 ping 的 RFID 技术。我们测试过，我们知道它能行。再说一次，这通常全都取决于那些……

turns.en: But can you just explain that it does not work in your stores? Actually, I don't know anything about this. Can you clarify that?
turns.zh: 但你能解释一下为什么它在你们店里不管用吗？其实我对此一无所知。你能说清楚吗？

turns.en: It's difficult.
turns.zh: 这有点难解释。

turns.en: The signals are blocked by the steel. That's typically the way it works in our stores. It's more passive technology like that. There is an active version of RFID.
turns.zh: 信号被钢铁挡住了。这通常就是它在我们店里的情况，更多是那种被动式技术。RFID 有一个主动式的版本。

turns.en: That's out there.
turns.zh: 那确实是存在的。

turns.en: But again, it's typically... And it's not like they're not coming down. I mean, tag costs are nil at this point. That's not really the issue. It is truly the hardware capabilities to be able to put it everywhere you want, to be able to read the way you want it to. It's still a very expensive technology to this point. Three years from now.
turns.zh: 但再说一次，这通常是……而且也不是说价格没在下降。我是说，标签成本到现在已经几乎为零了。那其实不是问题所在。真正的问题是硬件的能力，能不能把它装到你想要的每一个地方，能不能按你想要的方式去读取。到目前为止它仍然是一种非常昂贵的技术。三年之后……

turns.en: Who knows?
turns.zh: 谁知道呢？

turns.en: So why don't we talk about what happens after the goods get out of the retail environment? And maybe we should talk about the distribution environment at some point, too.
turns.zh: 那我们何不谈谈，当商品流出零售环境之后会发生什么？也许我们在某个时候也该谈谈配送环节。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: What is fencing? Not the sport.
turns.zh: 什么是销赃（fencing）？我不是说那项运动。

turns.en: So again, I kind of mentioned what we call the boosters. And we're specifically now talking about organized retail crime. Boosters are the people that do the stealing. Typically, they are recruited. They are given a list. They are given money. They are given, in many cases, drugs or the promise of drugs to when they come back with the product, which is kind of the hook to make sure that they don't just walk away with the product. And their money. And these folks are the ones that go out and they take the risk. They pull the product out of the stores and they do it. Like I said, they can be very aggressive. They could be very violent in many cases. And all they're thinking about is how do I get out of this building and go to where I'm supposed to go? And they take it to what we call the fence. The fence is kind of the consolidator of the product. So this could be somebody's house in their garage. This could be a warehouse facility. This could be a flea market.
turns.zh: 再说一次，我提到过我们所说的“booster”。而我们现在具体谈的是有组织零售犯罪。booster 就是实施盗窃的人。通常他们是被招募来的，会拿到一份清单，会拿到钱，很多情况下会拿到毒品、或者拿到毒品的承诺——等他们带着商品回来时兑现，这算是个钩子，确保他们不会带着商品和钱直接跑掉。这些人是出去、承担风险的人。他们把商品从店里弄出来。就像我说的，他们可能非常凶狠，很多情况下可能非常暴力。而他们脑子里想的只是：我怎么离开这栋楼、去我该去的地方？然后他们把货带给我们所说的“销赃者”（fence）。fence 算是商品的集散者。这可能是某人家的车库，可能是一个仓库设施，也可能是一个跳蚤市场。

turns.en: This could be you name it.
turns.zh: 可能是任何你能叫得出名字的地方。

turns.en: I'll get back to it. There's another interesting twist on this piece of it that I'll get back to what the boosters are doing and fences are doing here. But then these fences are the folks that actually clean the product and then offer the product for resale. So when I say clean it, to your point, some of these have electronic tags on them. They might have identifying, this is a product that's sold at Home Depot. This is a product that's sold at Target. This is a product sold at CVS. Stickers, identifying, price tags, things like that. They want to clean all that product. And then they'll offer it for sale somewhere. More and more since late teens, early 20s, that's online. In the past, I would say it was some of the bigger online folks, the Amazons of the world, the Ebays of the world, the bigger places. Since the Informed Consumers Act was passed in 2023, I believe is when it came effective. we've seen less of that on the bigger places. And now it's moved to more of the peer-to-peer markets. So the Craigslist, the Facebook marketplaces of the world, that's where a lot of that product is then offered for sale. And so that's the fencing operation. And then the money is then kicked up to wherever, or at least a portion of it, just like your traditional organized crime. It's kicked up to some bosses that are managing this whole operation from the top. And whether that's a Five guys that are sitting in an apartment or a house that just kind of decided that they want to be organized retail criminals certainly fits the definition of all those types of things. And they're using the money to furnish a lifestyle or a cartel or a Chinese transnational gang or a South American whatever. That could be any of those people that are the ones that are sitting at that top level. supervising the fences, making sure that the product's getting moved and making sure that the money's coming in.
turns.zh: 我待会儿还会回到这点。在这一块上还有一个有意思的转折，我回头再讲 booster 和 fence 在这里干的事。但接着，这些 fence 是真正给商品“清洗”、然后把商品拿去转卖的人。所以当我说清洗时，就像你说的，其中一些商品上有电子标签。它们可能带有标识——这是在 Home Depot 卖的商品、这是在 Target 卖的商品、这是在 CVS 卖的商品——贴纸、标识、价格标签之类的。他们想把所有这些商品都清洗干净。然后他们会在某个地方把它挂出来卖。从 2010 年代末、2020 年代初开始，越来越多是在线上。过去我会说，是在一些较大的线上平台，世界上那些 Amazon、那些 eBay，那些大平台。自 INFORM Consumers Act 于 2023 年通过——我记得是那时生效——以来，我们在那些大平台上看到的这类东西变少了。现在它转移到了更多的点对点（peer-to-peer）市场。所以是 Craigslist、世界上那些 Facebook Marketplace，很多这类商品随后就在那里挂出来卖。这就是销赃运作。然后钱会被上缴到某处，或者至少一部分会上缴，就像你传统意义上的有组织犯罪一样。它被上缴给某些从顶层管理着整个运作的头目。无论那是坐在某间公寓或某栋房子里、决定要当有组织零售罪犯的五个人——这当然符合所有那些类型的定义。他们用这些钱来供养一种生活方式，或者一个贩毒集团，或者一个中国的跨国帮派，或者某个南美的什么。可能是那些人当中的任何一个，坐在顶层，监督着这些 fence，确保商品被转移出去、确保钱源源进来。

turns.en: So I've heard, you know, there have been stories about Facebook Marketplace and frustration that Facebook hasn't done more. I'm not sure what the status of that, you know, if you see for sale on Facebook Marketplace, like a 10 pack of unopened Hanes t-shirts or something like that, There might be legitimate reason to think that this was stolen. It could also be a legitimate sale. Someone bought T-shirts and they never wore them like it's plausible. What is the optimal role for an owner of a peer-to-peer platform to play? And then what do you perceive right now is the gap between what would be a sort of like optimal role for them and contribution to fighting this versus what they're doing right now?
turns.zh: 我听说过，你知道，有一些关于 Facebook Marketplace 的报道，以及人们对 Facebook 没有做更多事的失望。我不确定那件事的现状。你知道，如果你在 Facebook Marketplace 上看到有人卖，比如一包 10 件、未拆封的 Hanes T 恤之类的，可能有正当理由认为这是偷来的。但也可能是一笔合法的交易：某人买了 T 恤，从来没穿过，这是说得通的。那么对一个点对点平台的所有者来说，最理想的角色是什么？然后你现在认为，在他们能扮演的理想角色、对打击这件事的贡献，与他们现在实际所做的之间，差距有多大？

turns.en: The short answer is it's very expensive to patrol your platform, to know your seller, to make sure that you really understand that they're a legitimate business and that they're a legitimate reseller. In form, the federal bill that was passed earlier required the traditional marketplaces to actually do that, take that step and make sure that they did. Just like I have to know who my suppliers are here at Home Depot, they had to know who their suppliers are at the Amazons and the Ebays of the world. There was a loophole in that bill that did not cover the peer-to-peer resellers. Can't explain why it happened, just it happened. And so that loophole has continued to exist for it. And they're not going to put the governance in to do it unless they're forced to, just like the bigger boxes didn't have to before InForm. And so we spend a lot of time governing those marketplaces. So we have technologies that are looking at that and say... If Home Depot sells this combination drill kit for $ 499, how in the heck is Tommy1234 selling it for $ 200 at volume? How can he sell new in-box product at a price lower than my cost? And so we will look for that type of stuff. And that's where a lot of our investigations also will start. We'll actually start on the marketplace and work backwards to the person coming into the store, going back to kind of our earlier discussion.
turns.zh: 简短的回答是，巡查你自己的平台、了解你的卖家、确保你真的明白他们是合法商家、是合法的转卖者，这非常昂贵。之前通过的那部联邦法案 INFORM，要求传统的市场平台真正去做这件事、迈出那一步、并确保做到。就像我在 Home Depot 必须知道我的供应商是谁一样，世界上那些 Amazon、那些 eBay 也必须知道他们的供应商是谁。但那部法案里有一个漏洞，没有覆盖点对点的转卖者。我没法解释为什么会这样，反正它就是发生了。所以这个漏洞一直存在。除非被迫，否则他们不会把治理机制放进去，就像在 INFORM 之前那些大平台不必做一样。所以我们花大量时间去治理那些市场。我们有技术去盯着这些，然后说……如果 Home Depot 卖这套组合电钻套装是 499 美元，Tommy1234 怎么可能大量地以 200 美元卖它？他怎么能以低于我成本的价格卖全新盒装商品？所以我们会去找这类东西。而我们很多调查也正是从这里开始的。我们实际上会从市场平台开始，反向追查，一直查到走进店里的那个人，这就回到了我们前面讨论的内容。

turns.en: But it's whack-a-mole to a certain degree, right?
turns.zh: 但这在某种程度上是打地鼠（whack-a-mole），对吧？

turns.en: I mean, we're really patrolling millions and millions of sellers that are out there. So we build criterias. We build models that kind of look and say, boy, this person sells a lot of drills. This person sells a lot of drills new in box. This person sells a lot of drills new in box under our cost for the product. So that's kind of the way we tend to do that. But it's an uphill climb. It's a big battle.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们真的要巡查外面数以百万计的卖家。所以我们建立各种标准，建立模型，去看、去判断：哇，这个人卖很多电钻；这个人卖很多全新盒装的电钻；这个人卖很多全新盒装、且低于我们商品成本的电钻。这就是我们通常的做法。但这是一场爬坡，是一场大战。

turns.en: This might be a very niche question, but do you observe any interesting trends when it comes to the prices that fences are actually choosing for these items? Because they could, I mean, if you have something new in a box, you could maybe try to charge almost full price for a power drill or something. Or you see them with like massive discounts as well, and they're leaving money on the table.
turns.zh: 这可能是个很小众的问题，但就销赃者实际为这些商品定的价格而言，你有没有观察到什么有意思的趋势？因为他们本可以——我是说，如果你有全新盒装的东西，也许可以试着对一把电钻之类收取几乎全价。或者你也会看到他们打巨大的折扣，那样就是把钱白白留在桌上了。

turns.en: I wouldn't tell you that I've done a lot of research into what the specifics are. What the general consensus is, the more technology-laden the product is, the more it sells closer to retail. That plus gift cards. Gift cards tend to sell very close to retail. So we see a lot of our products selling in the 70% to 80% of retail range. Whereas in some cases, you'd think about the deodorants and the t-shirts and the The Tylenol and some of that tends to be in the 30 to 40 cents per of retail market. So there's some broad strokes on that. But honestly, I don't spend a ton of time doing that. Just it tends to be like if it's Internet connected, it sells very, very close to retail. If it's technology driven, it's got some resale capability to it.
turns.zh: 我不会说我针对具体数字做过大量研究。一般的共识是：一件商品的技术含量越高，它卖得就越接近零售价。再加上礼品卡——礼品卡往往卖得非常接近零售价。所以我们看到我们很多商品在零售价的 70% 到 80% 区间成交。而有些情况下，你会想到除臭剂、T 恤、Tylenol 之类，这些往往落在零售价的 30% 到 40% 区间。所以这方面有一些大致的规律。但老实说，我没花太多时间研究这个。大致就是：如果它能联网，就卖得非常非常接近零售价；如果它是技术驱动的，就具备一定的转卖能力。

turns.en: Efficient markets finding the right price of anything on any platform. So you talk about this loophole in the law that allowed the peer to peer sellers. What would be that additional step? okay, if they were to close this loophole, what would they then be required to do? And are you either surprised or disappointed given, I mean, a company like Meta is gigantic. Are you either, would you have been surprised or a little disappointed that they would not feel the impulse to do this voluntarily without being required by law?
turns.zh: 有效市场（efficient markets）会在任何平台上为任何东西找到合适的价格。那你谈到法律里这个允许点对点卖家的漏洞。那额外的一步会是什么？好，如果他们要堵住这个漏洞，那他们就会被要求做什么？而且，考虑到像 Meta 这样的公司是巨无霸，你是感到惊讶还是失望——你会不会惊讶或有点失望，他们竟然没有那种冲动、在没有法律强制的情况下自愿去做这件事？

turns.en: They'll tell you that they do a lot of policing of their site. And I'm not arguing that they don't have... I know they have departments that do that.
turns.zh: 他们会告诉你，他们对自己的网站做了大量巡查。我也不是说他们没有……我知道他们有专门做这件事的部门。

turns.en: We work with them.
turns.zh: 我们跟他们合作。

turns.en: I mean, so they're not completely willfully blind. They're not completely out there just saying, no, it doesn't happen on our site. We think they could do more. And again, it comes back to if they had information, if they had policing in place that said, how in the world does this guy undercut Home Depot or Target on pricing? That should be a flag for them to say, I'm going to pull you off the site. I'm going to suspend you from the site versus us having to come to them and say, this guy is undercutting us on pricing. He's selling at volume. He's selling at scale. We've bought the product for it. We know what store it came from. We know that this guy's involved in crime.
turns.zh: 我是说，所以他们并不是完全在睁一只眼闭一只眼。他们并不是完全站在那里只说“不，这种事不会发生在我们的网站上”。我们认为他们可以做更多。而且这又回到：如果他们掌握了信息，如果他们建立了巡查机制，会说“这家伙到底是怎么在价格上压过 Home Depot 或 Target 的？”那对他们来说就应该是一个警示信号，让他们说“我要把你从网站上撤下来，我要封禁你”，而不是非得由我们去找他们说“这家伙在价格上压过我们，他在大量卖、在规模化地卖，我们买过他的商品，我们知道那来自哪家店，我们知道这个人卷入了犯罪”。

turns.en: Now you go pull them off the site.
turns.zh: 然后再由你去把他们从网站上撤下来。

turns.en: And so your answer is both disappointed and surprised.
turns.zh: 所以你的答案是既失望又惊讶。

turns.en: Do I think they could be doing more? For sure.
turns.zh: 我觉得他们能做更多吗？当然。

turns.en: Do I think that I should be the one that has to come? It seems a little backwards to me that I should have to come and tell them that they've got somebody selling stolen product on their site versus them knowing who their suppliers are, knowing that tax records exist and that there's filings that are out there that they should be held accountable to the same way the Amazons and the Ebays of the world are.
turns.zh: 我觉得该由我出面吗？在我看来这有点本末倒置：竟然要我去告诉他们，他们的网站上有人在卖赃物，而不是由他们自己去了解他们的供应商是谁、知道税务记录的存在、知道外面有那些申报文件，他们应该像世界上那些 Amazon、那些 eBay 一样为此负责。

turns.en: Can you talk a little bit more about the balance between trying to shrink the shrink in various ways and customer experience. Because again, we've all experienced the frustration of going into, usually it's a drugstore of some kind and hitting the plastic wall and having to press the button and wait for someone to come and then You're standing there for 10 minutes and then they don't have the right key. And sorry, this happened to me recently.
turns.zh: 你能多谈谈吗，在想方设法降低损耗和顾客体验之间的平衡。因为话说回来，我们都有过那种挫败经历：走进一家店——通常是某种药店——撞上一道塑料墙，不得不按下按钮、等人过来，然后你在那儿站上 10 分钟，结果他们还没有对的钥匙。抱歉，这件事最近就发生在我身上。

turns.en: No, keep going on. So they don't have the right key.
turns.zh: 不，你继续说。所以他们没有对的钥匙。

turns.en: I get a few of those emails every week from our from our leadership. So I got to.
turns.zh: 我每周都会从我们的领导层那里收到几封那样的邮件。所以我得……

turns.en: But stores, some stores have clearly made the decision that it's worth it to them economically to do this.
turns.zh: 但一些门店，有些门店显然已经做出了决定：从经济上看，这么做对他们是值得的。

turns.en: We have. It is not an easy conversation with your merchants. It's not an easy conversation with your operators. It's a very arduous data-driven discussion. And so I can think back when I got here in 2018, middle of 2018, and we were on a trajectory of shrink that was not good. It was going way the wrong way at that point. And we started to have some of these conversations. But I'm a data guy and I'm a test and learn guy. I like to have my facts. And so we did some testing.
turns.zh: 我们也做了。这跟你的采购/商品团队（merchants）不是一场轻松的对话，跟你的运营团队（operators）也不是一场轻松的对话。这是一场非常艰难、由数据驱动的讨论。所以我可以回想，2018 年、2018 年年中我刚到这里时，我们的损耗处在一个不好的轨迹上，当时正朝完全错误的方向走。于是我们开始进行其中一些讨论。但我是一个数据派、一个“测试并学习”（test and learn）派的人，我喜欢掌握事实。所以我们做了一些测试。

turns.en: We did this.
turns.zh: 我们做了这件事。

turns.en: We did a lot of looking into what products we were losing very, very specifically under the microscope. We found that one particular combination of kit that we were selling for $ 799, we would buy it 4.2 times for every time we sell it.
turns.zh: 我们非常非常具体地、放在显微镜下研究我们在丢哪些商品。我们发现，有一套特定的组合套装我们卖 799 美元，每卖出一次，我们就要采购它 4.2 次。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: Now, go have that conversation with your finance folks. And they go, that's a gross margin mix we don't like. That's a real business opportunity. If you can get me to break even, if you can get me to slightly positive on that, you know, from a gross margin perspective, then they go, OK, there's a little bit of a tradeoff. But it's also we're in a unique business. We're in a business that 50% of our revenue comes from pros and contractors. If they leave a job site because their drill broke and they go to the store because it said we had one and we don't, that's a problem too. And so, you know, as we kind of walked through and we worked through this, we got to a very curated list of products where we said, We're going to probably have to do something. And if we do it, we can do it the right way and try to minimize the friction. We use QR codes on all of our lockups that summon somebody through our phone that they come. And it takes, on average, about 90 seconds for that lockup to be unlocked by a person. I want to be in a place where customers can self-service. If they scan the QR code and I know that they're a pro that's in our loyalty program, Why can't I give them access to that? So we're working through the friction. That's always going to be an opportunity for us. And we're trying to minimize it to the best we can. But it's not perfect. And it's definitely a little bit of a balancing act that you walk on some of those particular products. You can't do everything. That's just buy online. If that exists, that's Amazon. If you don't want to go into a store and you don't want to be held up and you can wait three hours to get a product, go to Amazon. That's something we do. Thankfully, they don't necessarily operate in our space. Don't sell power drills like we do.
turns.zh: 现在，去跟你的财务团队谈这个。他们会说，这是我们不喜欢的毛利率结构（gross margin mix）。这是一个真正的商业机会。如果你能让我打平，如果你能让我在毛利率上稍微转正，那么他们会说，好，这里面有一点权衡。但也因为，我们处在一个独特的行业。我们的业务里有 50% 的收入来自专业人士和承包商（pros and contractors）。如果他们因为电钻坏了而离开工地，来到店里，因为系统显示我们有货、结果我们却没有，那也是个问题。所以，你知道，随着我们一步步梳理、把这个过程走完，我们得出了一份非常精心挑选的商品清单，我们说：对这些商品我们大概得做点什么。而如果我们做，我们可以用正确的方式做，并尽量减少摩擦。我们在所有的防盗锁盒（lockups）上都用二维码（QR code），通过手机呼叫某人过来。平均而言，一个人来把那个锁盒打开大约需要 90 秒。我想做到让顾客能自助。如果他们扫二维码，而我知道他们是加入我们忠诚计划的专业人士，为什么我不能给他们开放权限？所以我们正在解决这个摩擦问题。这对我们永远都是一个课题，我们在尽力把它降到最低。但它并不完美。在某些特定商品上，这绝对是一种需要拿捏的平衡。你没法什么都做。如果那样，那干脆就网上买——如果那种需求存在，那就是 Amazon。如果你不想走进店里、不想被卡住、可以等三个小时才拿到商品，那就去 Amazon。那是我们做的取舍。谢天谢地，他们不一定在我们这个领域经营，不像我们这样卖电钻。

turns.en: Do you notice that sales actually go down for items that have been locked up?
turns.zh: 你有没有注意到，那些被锁起来的商品，销量实际上会下降？

turns.en: Not necessarily.
turns.zh: 不一定。

turns.en: There are some categories where that is true. There's also many, many categories where actually sales go up because you're in stock.
turns.zh: 有些品类确实如此。但也有很多很多品类，销量实际上是上升的，因为你有货。

turns.en: That's interesting.
turns.zh: 这很有意思。

turns.en: I hadn't thought about that, but that makes a ton of sense. It's funny when I go into pharmacies and it's all locked up, I always say to myself, oh, I'm just going to start shopping online for all this stuff. But I never actually do. I'm always back at the pharmacy, like, every week. But I am curious. You mentioned Omni. Like, what is the sort of modal mode of. Shrink when we're talking about the e-commerce context?
turns.zh: 我之前没想到这一点，但这非常有道理。有意思的是，当我走进药店、发现东西全锁起来时，我总是对自己说，哦，我以后干脆都在网上买这些东西好了。但我其实从来没这么做。我总是每周又回到药店。但我很好奇。你提到了全渠道（Omni）。那么，当我们谈电商这个语境时，损耗最常见的那种形态（modal mode）是什么？

turns.en: There's a couple of ways.
turns.zh: 有那么几种方式。

turns.en: I mean, a lot of this falls back to payments fraud, you know, credit card fraud, gift card fraud. You know, the payment process oftentimes is the way that they're defrauding the Omni space. There's a, to use your word, a niche piece of people buying product taking the product out, using it, putting something back in and then doing returns. So they get back on the return side. So they're getting credits for the product that they actually have and then send back to get their full refund price on. So that's a part of the business that we deal with in many cases that we're working through. But it's typically around the payment side and the gift card and credit card fraud.
turns.zh: 我是说，这里面很多要归结到支付欺诈（payments fraud），你知道，信用卡欺诈、礼品卡欺诈。支付环节往往就是他们欺诈全渠道这块的方式。还有一个——用你的词说——一个小众的部分：有人买下商品，把商品拿出去、用掉，再往里塞点别的东西，然后办理退货。所以他们在退货这一侧把钱拿回来。他们为实际上还留在自己手里的商品拿到退款额度，然后把替换的东西寄回去，以拿到全额退款。所以这是我们很多情况下要处理、正在解决的一部分业务。但它通常是围绕支付这一侧，以及礼品卡和信用卡欺诈。

turns.en: Isn't there some like e-commerce like incidents for people where they They're like, I want to return this and they'll get the refund and they're like, but don't bother sending it back. It's not worth it for the ingest.
turns.zh: 难道没有那种电商的情况吗，就是有人说“我要退这个”，然后他们拿到退款，平台却说“不用麻烦寄回来了，走入库流程不划算”。

turns.en: Oh, sure.
turns.zh: 哦，当然有。

turns.en: Yeah. Sure.
turns.zh: 是啊，当然。

turns.en: I realize we've been very focused on the retail side of theft, but can you talk a little bit more about what happens on the back end with distribution? Because, of course, you know, you're shipping a bunch of stuff from its production center over to the store itself. I imagine there are many, many avenues along the way that a smart criminal could exploit.
turns.zh: 我意识到我们一直非常聚焦在盗窃的零售这一侧，但你能多谈谈后端配送环节发生的事吗？因为，当然了，你要把一大堆货从生产中心运到门店本身。我想这一路上有很多很多渠道，是聪明的罪犯可以利用的。

turns.en: Yeah, it's growing, to be honest with you.
turns.zh: 是啊，说实话，它在增长。

turns.en: I think there's, I would say, three main modes, go back to the modal piece of it, but there is pure diversion. So whether that's en route from vendor into, if you're an importer that bring it into the US, you go into your transload facilities, your port facilities, there's people that divert full trailer loads back someplace else from that port, could be back onto a container ship to go right back over someplace else that's been stolen.
turns.zh: 我想有——我会说——三种主要形态，回到那个“最常见形态”的话题。有一种是纯粹的转运劫持（diversion）。所以无论是在从供应商运进来的途中，如果你是一个把货运进美国的进口商，货进入你的换装（transload）设施、你的港口设施，就有人把整整一拖车的货从那个港口改道运到别处，可能被重新装上一艘集装箱船、直接运回另一个地方，这些货就被偷走了。

turns.en: There are breaking.
turns.zh: 还有一种是闯入。

turns.en: In terms of actually just as truck drivers drive eight hours across country and they got to park their trailer somewhere. And during the time they're sleeping, they're breaking into the back of the trailer and just taking the boxes off the back. And then there's the one you mentioned a little bit earlier, which is the diversion on the supply chain side back out. So we're seeing a lot of fraudulent bill of lading, fraudulent pickup paperwork. AI is playing a space in this where they're able to duplicate some of the capacities that allow a driver to just drive straight in and say, I'm here to pick up trailer 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. And they dribble right out because their paperwork looks really real. Now, we're moving away from that with the electronic billing and some of the new ways that we're.
turns.zh: 就是那种，卡车司机在全国开了八个小时，总得把拖车停在某个地方。而在他们睡觉的时候，有人撬开拖车后部，直接把箱子从后面搬走。然后还有你前面提到一点的那种，就是供应链这一侧把货反向劫持出去。所以我们看到大量伪造的提货单（bill of lading）、伪造的提货文件。AI 在这个领域正扮演角色，他们能够复制出某些能力，让一个司机直接把车开进来说“我是来提 1、2、3、4、5 号拖车的”，然后就这么把货开出去，因为他们的文件看起来非常真。现在，我们正在用电子单据（electronic billing）和一些新的方式摆脱这种情况，我们正在……

turns.en: Dealing with it.
turns.zh: 处理它。

turns.en: It's not necessarily the scheme that's new. It's the volume that seems to be new because it's a very difficult thing to go after. Rail has become an issue. Rail has definitely become a bigger issue over the last probably five or six years where we're seeing, you know, as the cars are parked in yards, they're being broken into by mobs of people that just kind of strip them down for what's in it. But they have really good intelligence, which is interesting. So, you know, we think They have people working inside the companies, the shipping companies, the trucking companies, because they don't hit every trailer or every car on the rail. They hit the car on the rail that has the product that they really want to go after. And so whether that's firearms, whether that's electronics, connected devices, you name it, there's a lot of, I would say, kind of a new– opening up on the rail space. And a lot of dead track, by the way, out there, too. So, like, it's wide open.
turns.zh: 不一定是手法在翻新，看起来是数量在翻新，因为这是很难去追查的事情。铁路已经成了一个问题。在过去大概五六年里，铁路肯定变成了一个更大的问题。我们看到，当车厢停在调车场里时，它们被成群的人撬开，把里面的东西洗劫一空。但他们拥有非常好的情报，这很有意思。所以，你知道，我们认为他们在这些公司内部有人——航运公司、卡车运输公司——因为他们不会去动每一节拖车或铁轨上的每一节车厢，他们只动铁轨上那节装着他们真正想要的商品的车厢。所以无论是枪支、电子产品、联网设备，你能叫得出名字的，我会说铁路这块正在打开很多新的口子。而且顺便说一句，外面有很多废弃轨道（dead track）。所以，就像，那里是完全敞开的。

turns.en: It's interesting you mentioned, you know, showing up with a fake invoice or a fake bill of lading. I wonder if you, like, put on an orange smock, et cetera, like, how much, you know, you just, like, just blend right in and, like, fit in and no one... No, I'm sure people are trained to be suspicious. But you mentioned AI. Like, how much of, like, the tools... I'm sure there's, you know, we talked about cameras that could theoretically detect when someone has put something in a pocket, et cetera. But the tools that we call AI, like, have you found uses for them in, I guess, sort of offensive deployment, whether the models can autonomously just scan through Facebook marketplaces and look for anything that we at Home Depot had found suspicious. How much sort of have you found that the models can be sort of applied towards general tasks and find helpful info for you?
turns.zh: 有意思的是你提到，你知道，带着假发票或假提货单出现。我想知道，如果你比如套上一件橙色工作服之类的，你能在多大程度上就……直接融入进去、混进去，没人察觉……不，我相信人们是受过训练要保持警惕的。但你提到了 AI。那么，那些我们称之为 AI 的工具，你在多大程度上发现了它们的用处——我猜是那种进攻性的部署，比如模型能不能自主地去扫遍 Facebook Marketplace，寻找任何我们 Home Depot 觉得可疑的东西。你在多大程度上发现，这些模型可以被应用到通用任务上、为你找到有用的信息？

turns.en: Yeah, look, I'll say it this way.
turns.zh: 是啊，看，我会这么说。

turns.en: We have more cases than we can investigate. And so for us, it's an efficiency play, right? So the more we can shorten the duration of these cases, like our typical ORC case takes about 70 days from discovery to closure to handing off to the police department. And so if we can compress that timeframe, we can turn more. And so we believe that the video... We just replaced our entire video analytics, our video management system in all 2,300 stores to an upgraded version that allows us to now put edge analytics on our cameras, the ones we have. Doesn't get necessarily to the point where you're talking about where... This action or this set of actions now becomes suspicious and identify somebody. We'll get to that. There's a place for that. I just don't have enough cameras in all my stores to do that. But the cameras that I do have, we are putting edge analytics around there that help us identify persons that were walking in this store and they were lingering in this space too long or they were avoiding associates or they were in a place where they shouldn't have been. That's definitely out there. You mentioned the web crawling.
turns.zh: 我们手上的案子比我们能调查的还多。所以对我们来说，这是一个效率的问题，对吧？我们越能缩短这些案子的时长——比如我们典型的一起有组织零售犯罪（ORC）案子，从发现到结案、到移交给警察部门，大约要 70 天。所以如果我们能压缩这个时间段，我们就能处理更多案子。因此我们相信视频……我们刚刚把所有 2,300 家门店的整套视频分析、视频管理系统，替换成了一个升级版本，让我们现在可以在我们已有的摄像头上部署边缘分析（edge analytics）。它不一定能达到你所说的那个程度，就是“这个动作或这一组动作现在变得可疑、并识别出某个人”。我们会做到那一步，那里有它的用武之地。只是我所有门店里的摄像头还不够多，做不到那一点。但我确实拥有的那些摄像头，我们正在其周围部署边缘分析，帮我们识别那些走进这家店、在某个区域逗留太久、或者刻意避开员工、或者出现在他们不该出现的地方的人。那确实是存在的。你提到了网络爬取（web crawling）。

turns.en: That's out there. That capability is out there.
turns.zh: 那是存在的，那种能力是存在的。

turns.en: We have our own company that does web crawling and identifies these things that absolutely looks for all that. So anything we can do to kind of compress that investigative cycle is how we're using AI to deploy against the bad actors that are out there today.
turns.zh: 我们有自己的公司做网络爬取、识别这些东西，绝对会去搜寻所有这些。所以任何我们能做的、用来压缩那个调查周期的事情，就是我们如何利用 AI 去对付今天外面那些坏人的方式。

turns.en: You know, obviously, like shoplifting theft, it affects all of us. It hurts your profit. It hurts my experience. It probably raises my prices, etc. There is a cost that we have to pay for taxes to increase the amount of police capacity, etc. This is a classic example of very bad externalities for almost everyone involved. And yet, you know, we see like this sort of like public backlash towards video cameras and so forth. There's been the last month, everyone's talking about the flock cameras, et cetera. What do you perceive as the sort of appetite among law enforcement or the politicians that would have to set laws to actually move the dial, et cetera, on some of this today in 2026?
turns.zh: 你知道，显然，像入店行窃这类盗窃，它影响我们所有人。它损害你的利润，损害我的购物体验，可能还抬高我的价格，等等。还有一种成本是我们必须通过纳税来支付，以增加警力的容量，等等。这是一个经典的例子，对几乎所有相关方来说都是极坏的负外部性（externalities）。然而，你知道，我们看到公众对视频监控摄像头之类有一种反弹。过去这一个月，人人都在谈论 Flock 摄像头等等。那么在 2026 年的今天，你觉得执法部门、或者那些必须立法才能真正推动局面改变的政客们，对这件事有多大的意愿（appetite）？

turns.en: Well, what I would tell you is I am super bullish on where this is going. We talked about INFORM, which was probably the first major ORC-driven act out there. We are now working on COORCA. COORCA is the Combating Organized Retail Crime Act. We are Home Depot. Retail in general has been a supporter. This is actually a very bipartisan act. It's passed the House. It has been attached to the NDAA. It's waiting on the Senate to sign it or to pass it. The president will sign it. He's already indicated that he will. This is like literally the first organized retail crime act at the federal level that provides resources, prosecutors, coordination centers, defines changes to USC 182314 that says here's how you have dedicated federal resources to go after this. Here's the issue. This is not a local crime. This is not a– it happens in the county of Cobb here in Georgia. It goes to Cobb, and it goes outside the state of Georgia, and it goes into South Carolina, and it goes into North Carolina. That is now a federal crime. This is interstate commerce. This is interstate transportation of stolen goods. all these things, yet there's no federal resources dedicated to this. So this gets ORC, this gets cargo theft, this gets gift card and payments fraud, all wrapped into one bill that is going to really change the way we as retailers can address this problem of organized crime. So The short answer is absolutely, I think the tide is changing. It's not just one-sided. There's, I want to say, 100 to maybe 200-plus House sponsors, both from the Democrat and Republican side. There are many, many bipartisan sponsors in the Senate for Cawarca. There are 35-ish states that have organized retail crime task forces led by their attorneys general, both in Democrat and Republican states. So, Seven years ago, I was doom and gloom on this. Nobody was taking this seriously. Nobody thought this was a big problem. This was petty shoplifting. This was not a thing that anybody really wanted to go on. In fact, in many cases, I think you guys know, it was decriminalization was happening. Lots of defunding, the police talk that was out there. I think that this has helped us move much more in the right direction over the last couple of years, particularly.
turns.zh: 嗯，我会告诉你，我对这件事的走向超级看好。我们谈到了 INFORM，那可能是第一部由有组织零售犯罪（ORC）驱动的重大法案。我们现在正在推动 COORCA。COORCA 就是《打击有组织零售犯罪法案》（Combating Organized Retail Crime Act）。我们 Home Depot、以及整个零售业一直是支持者。这其实是一部非常跨党派（bipartisan）的法案。它已经通过了众议院，被附加到了《国防授权法》（NDAA）上，正等着参议院签署或通过。总统会签署它，他已经表示会签。这几乎就是联邦层面第一部有组织零售犯罪法案，它提供资源、检察官、协调中心，界定了对 USC 182314 的修改，说明你将拥有专门的联邦资源去打击这件事。问题在这里：这不是一起本地犯罪。它不是……它发生在 Georgia 州的 Cobb 县，然后走出 Cobb，走出 Georgia 州，进入 South Carolina，再进入 North Carolina。那现在就是一项联邦犯罪。这是州际商务（interstate commerce），这是被盗商品的州际运输，所有这些东西，然而却没有专门投入的联邦资源。所以这部法案把 ORC、把货物盗窃、把礼品卡和支付欺诈，全都打包进一部法案，它将真正改变我们作为零售商应对这个有组织犯罪问题的方式。所以简短的回答是：绝对的，我认为风向正在改变。它不是单边的。我想说，众议院有 100 到也许 200 多位提案人，来自民主党和共和党两边。参议院有非常非常多的跨党派提案人支持 COORCA。有大约 35 个州已经成立了由各州总检察长（attorneys general）牵头的有组织零售犯罪专案组，民主党和共和党执政的州都有。所以，七年前，我对这件事是悲观失望的。没人把它当回事，没人认为这是个大问题。这被认为是小小偷小摸，不是任何人真正想去追查的事。事实上，很多情况下——我想你们也知道——当时正在发生非罪化（decriminalization），有很多削减警费的言论。我认为这帮助我们在过去这几年、尤其是最近，朝着正确的方向前进了很多。

turns.en: What is the state of the art with facial recognition? What are the expectations that people should know when they're like walking into a major public space, the degree to which either the cameras in major retail establishments either are able to or are able to identify who they are and how long that data is stored and so forth?
turns.zh: 人脸识别（facial recognition）目前的最先进水平是怎样的？当人们走进一个大型公共场所时，他们应该知道些什么样的预期——大型零售场所里的摄像头在多大程度上能够识别出他们是谁，以及这些数据会被存储多久，等等？

turns.en: That's a conversation that could probably go for another two hours. I would say that at the end of the day, video analytics in general are getting really, really good about recognizing people. And we don't talk about specific technologies that are out there. I'm not an expert in facial recognition, so I don't know. What I would say is that... fair to have conversations about misuse. It's fair to have conversations about balancing the good versus the bad that can come from any technology that's out there. But I'm probably not the person to really talk about facial recognition.
turns.zh: 那可能是一场还能再聊上两个小时的对话。我会说，归根结底，视频分析总体上在识别人这方面正变得非常非常好。我们不谈论外面那些具体的技术。我不是人脸识别方面的专家，所以我不知道。我要说的是……谈论滥用是合理的，谈论在好与坏之间取得平衡也是合理的——任何外面的技术都会带来好与坏。但我可能不是那个真正适合谈人脸识别的人。

turns.en: All right, Scott Glenn, thank you so much for coming on All Thoughts. Really appreciate it.
turns.zh: 好，Scott Glenn，非常感谢你来上 Odd Lots。真的很感激。

turns.en: No, thanks for the time. I appreciate you guys.
turns.zh: 不，谢谢你们的时间。我很感激你们。

turns.en: So, Joe, that was a fascinating conversation. It definitely helped me understand the whole lockup issue. I hadn't considered that. I kind of assumed that sales would go down because so many people would be inconvenienced and you just walk away and say, whatever, I'm going to get my toothbrush from Amazon. But if the inventory isn't there anyway because people are stealing it, then that's a lost opportunity for sale. The other thing that stood out for me is there are some slightly dystopian aspects in there. So the idea of videos with edge capabilities might be looking at your behavior and classifying this person as a risk. Like, oh, this person has been standing over in that corner for a while, looks kind of suspicious. That doesn't sound great. The other thing that was very briefly mentioned is this idea that Well, maybe there's a way around the lockup program where you could just scan a QR code from your, you know, I don't know, Walmart or Home Depot loyalty app. And it would automatically open the shelf for you.
turns.zh: 那么，Joe，那真是一场引人入胜的对话。它确实帮我理解了整个“锁盒”（lockup）的问题。我之前没考虑到这点。我原以为销量会下降，因为那么多人会嫌麻烦，你干脆走开、说“算了，我去 Amazon 买我的牙刷”。但如果反正因为有人偷、货架上根本没有库存，那这就是一次错失的销售机会。另一件让我印象深刻的是，这里面有一些略微反乌托邦（dystopian）的方面。比如，带有边缘能力的视频可能会盯着你的行为、把这个人归类为风险，就像“哦，这个人在那个角落站了好一会儿，看起来有点可疑”。这听起来不太妙。另一件被非常简短提到的事，是这个想法：嗯，也许有一种绕过锁盒方案的办法，你只要从你的、我不知道、Walmart 或 Home Depot 的忠诚度 App 上扫一个二维码，货架就会自动为你打开。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Which sounds very convenient. Not very convenient, but more convenient if you're a shopper, a regular shopper at those stores. But on the other hand, you're kind of getting close to an almost identity system for shopping.
turns.zh: 这听起来非常方便。倒不是非常方便，但如果你是那些店的常客，就会更方便一些。但另一方面，你就有点接近于为购物建立一套几乎等同于身份系统（identity system）的东西了。

turns.en: All great points. But yes, you know, it does feel like we're probably going to increasingly be headed in that direction, that whether we want to or not, the technology itself will be the driver. Like if edge AI works, if you could just have a model embedded onto the camera itself that could just say, identify suspicious behavior in real time, it will be implemented, right? Like there is, people might complain, but if the technology exists, it will eventually be implemented. I'm very anti-shoplifting. So I think like, you know, and like, I don't really, I think, you know, things would be better if there were less of it, et cetera. And I'm not particularly worried about like, well, if I'm in a public space.
turns.zh: 都是很好的观点。但是的，你知道，感觉上我们大概会越来越朝那个方向走，无论我们愿不愿意，技术本身就将是驱动力。比如，如果边缘 AI（edge AI）行得通，如果你能把一个模型直接嵌入摄像头本身，让它实时识别可疑行为，那它就会被部署，对吧？人们也许会抱怨，但只要技术存在，它最终就会被部署。我非常反对入店行窃。所以我想，你知道，我觉得如果这种事少一些，世界会更好，等等。而且我并不特别担心，嗯，如果我身处一个公共场所的话。

turns.en: But what if you just want to stand around for a couple hours admiring the power.
turns.zh: 但如果你只是想在那儿站上几个小时、欣赏那些电动……

turns.en: Tools without being harassed? No, look, there are obviously clear issues that are going to arise and they're going to be very uncomfortable and unsettling. But I believe that the technology will lead the way rather than anything that we prioritize.
turns.zh: ……工具，而不被骚扰吗？不，你看，显然会有一些明确的问题冒出来，而且它们会让人非常不自在、非常不安。但我相信，将会领路的是技术，而不是我们优先看重的任何东西。

turns.en: Here's the thing. I think the question you have to ask of the technology is whether it leads to... Good outcomes in the forms of more people being caught because part of this is like, OK, you can install surveillance in the store. You can stick tags on every individual item. But if security can't actually stop people from exiting the store with stolen goods because of liability issues, then. It's not really doing that much, right? Maybe it'll help in the investigation, but then you're still dependent on a potentially strained police force actually taking up the case and using the evidence that you've gathered.
turns.zh: 问题是这样的。我认为你必须对技术提出的问题，是它是否能带来……好的结果，即更多人被抓住，因为这里面一部分是：好，你可以在店里安装监控，你可以给每一件单独的商品都贴上标签。但如果保安因为责任问题实际上无法阻止人们带着赃物走出店门，那么，它其实没起多大作用，对吧？也许它会有助于调查，但那样你仍然要依赖一支可能已经捉襟见肘的警力，去真正接手这个案子、使用你收集到的证据。

turns.en: It does feel, he used the term whack-a-mole, and I feel like one of the meta-phenomenons that has happened is over time shoplifting or theft. has switched on these various online frauds, et cetera. But you would think like, oh, well, if you just get rid of the retail stores, then that takes care of the problem. But the crime finds a way and new forms of crime will emerge. And one day we'll probably have robot security guards who don't have like a personal safety issue because it's a robot and they'll like reach out and apprehend the person. But then there will be a theft on the robot supply chain and so forth. And like it'll probably never go away. But it was interesting.
turns.zh: 确实感觉如此——他用了“打地鼠”（whack-a-mole）这个词。我觉得已经发生的一个元现象（meta-phenomenon）是，随着时间推移，入店行窃或盗窃已经切换到了这些各种线上欺诈等等。但你会想，哦，那如果你干脆把实体零售店都干掉，问题不就解决了？但犯罪总会找到出路，新形式的犯罪会冒出来。有一天我们大概会有机器人保安，它们不存在人身安全问题，因为它就是个机器人，会伸手把那个人抓住。但那样机器人供应链上又会出现盗窃，等等。所以它大概永远不会消失。但这确实很有意思。

turns.en: Maybe the robots will need liability insurance. You don't know.
turns.zh: 也许机器人会需要责任保险（liability insurance）。这可说不准。

turns.en: They very well might.
turns.zh: 它们很可能真需要。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: But the robots will be shoplifters. That's right. The misaligned robot security guard.
turns.zh: 但机器人自己也会成为入店行窃者。没错。那个目标错位的机器人保安。

turns.en: That bolt over there is really shiny.
turns.zh: 那边那颗螺栓真的好亮。

turns.en: Yeah, that's right. All right. Shall we leave it there? Let's leave it there.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。好。我们就聊到这儿吧？就聊到这儿。
